explain.title: What is a statement?
explain.body: A sentence or mathematical expression which may be true or false but not both is called a statement. For example, 3 + 4 = 8 is a statement, and it is false.

explain.title: True and false statements
explain.body: A mathematical statement has one truth value: true or false. “The sum of the measures of the interior angles of a triangle is 180°” is true; “The set of integers is finite” is false.

explain.title: Induction and deduction
explain.body: Induction draws a general conclusion from a limited number of observations or repeated experiments. Deduction draws a conclusion from accepted or well-known facts.

explain.title: Axiom, conjecture and theorem
explain.body: An axiom is accepted as true without proof. A conjecture is proposed as true but has not been proved. A theorem is established by proof. Your textbook treats the straight-line fact as an axiom, the even-number-and-primes claim as a conjecture, and the triangle angle result as a theorem.

explain.title: How to prove an algebraic identity
explain.body: To show L.H.S. = R.H.S., start with one side, usually L.H.S., simplify one step at a time, and finish by reaching R.H.S. For example, expand squares and then combine like terms.

mistakes: Calling a question or command a statement: it does not assert something that is true or false.

explain.title: Negation
explain.body: If p is any statement, its negation is denoted by ~p, read ‘not p’. If p is true, ~p is false; if p is false, ~p is true.

explain.title: Conjunction
explain.body: The conjunction of two statements p and q is symbolically written as p ∧ q (p and q). A conjunction is considered to be true only if both statements are true.

explain.title: Disjunction
explain.body: The disjunction of p and q is symbolically written as p ∨ q (p or q). The disjunction p ∨ q is considered to be true when at least one of the statements is true. It is false when both of them are false.

explain.title: Conditional
explain.body: A compound statement of the form if p then q (p → q) also written as p implies q is called a conditional or an implication. p is called the antecedent or hypothesis and q is called the consequent or the conclusion. A conditional is regarded as false only when the antecedent is true and the consequent is false.

explain.title: Biconditional and related conditionals
explain.body: The statement p → q ∧ q → p is shortly written as p ↔ q and is called the biconditional or equivalence. It is read p iff q (iff stands for “if and only if”). For p → q, q → p is the converse, ~p → ~q is the inverse, and ~q → ~p is the contrapositive.

mistakes: Writing the converse when the question asks for the contrapositive: the contrapositive both swaps and negates the two parts.
Forgetting that the negation of ~p is p.
Marking p → q false whenever q is false. It is false only when p is true and q is false.
Treating p ∨ q as true only when both statements are true; that is the condition for a conjunction, not a disjunction.
Leaving out one of the four p, q combinations in a truth table.
Evaluating the final truth-table column before completing the inner operations.

explain.title: Theorem
explain.body: A theorem is a mathematical statement that has been proved true based on previously known facts. For example, the sum of the interior angles of a quadrilateral is 360 degrees.

explain.title: Conjecture
explain.body: A conjecture is a mathematical statement or hypothesis that is believed to be true based on observations but has not yet been proved. If it is proved true, it becomes a theorem; if it is disproved, it is false. The Goldbach Conjecture says every even integer greater than 2 is a sum of two prime numbers.

explain.title: Axiom
explain.body: An axiom is a mathematical statement that we believe to be true without any evidence or requiring any proof. In other words, these statements are basic facts that form the starting point for further ideas and are based on everyday experiences. Moreover, there is no evidence contradicting these statements. For example, through a given point, infinitely many lines can pass.

explain.title: Postulate
explain.body: Axioms are sometimes referred to as postulates. Both Axioms and Postulates describe statements that are accepted as true without requiring proof. However, postulates are associated explicitly with geometry, while axioms can pertain to broader mathematical contexts.

explain.title: What deductive reasoning means
explain.body: Deductive reasoning draws a conclusion from premises believed to be true. If the premises are true, the conclusion must also be true. For example, if all human beings need to breathe to live and Ahmad is a human, we conclude that Ahmad also needs to breathe to live.

explain.title: Deductive proof in algebra
explain.body: Deductive proof in an algebraic expression is a technique to show the validity of a mathematical statement through logical reasoning based on known rules, theorems, axioms, or previously proven statements. Each line of a proof should follow from a valid rule or an earlier line.

explain.title: How to prove an identity
explain.body: Start with one side, usually the L.H.S. Expand or simplify it by valid steps until it matches the R.H.S. A proof is complete when you show L.H.S. = R.H.S. and state that the result is hence proved.

explain.title: Justifying steps
explain.body: When asked to justify each step, name the rule that allows the change. For instance, division by a number can be written as multiplication by its reciprocal, and factors common to numerator and denominator can be cancelled when they are non-zero.

mistakes: Starting with the R.H.S. and changing both sides at once makes it harder to show that the identity follows logically.
Skipping algebraic steps or giving an incorrect reason can lose method marks even if the final answer is right.
Forgetting that a minus sign outside brackets changes every sign inside the brackets leads to incorrect expansions.
Cancelling terms across addition or subtraction is not valid; cancel common factors only.
In an odd/even proof, do not just say the result looks odd or even. Show it as 2k + 1 or 2k, where the remaining expression is an integer.

notes.title: Mathematical statements
notes.answer: A statement is a sentence or mathematical expression which may be true or false but not both.
notes.explanation: A statement is a sentence or mathematical expression that is either true or false, but not both. For example, “3 + 4 = 8” is a false statement, while “The sum of the interior angles of a triangle is 180°” is a true statement. A proof is a chain of logical steps that shows why a statement is true.
notes.simple: A statement makes a claim that can be judged true or false. A proof gives reasons, step by step, to show that a claim is true.
examples: The sum of the interior angles of a triangle is 180° is a true statement.
steps: Check whether the sentence makes a definite claim.
Ask whether the claim can be true or false, but not both.
If it does, it is a statement; then decide whether it is true or false.

notes.title: Reading and using logical operators
notes.answer: The five operators shown in your textbook are negation (~), conjunction (∧), disjunction (∨), conditional (→), and equivalence (↔).
notes.explanation: Logical operators connect statements or change their meaning. The main symbols are negation (~), and (∧), or (∨), implication (→), and equivalence (↔). A conditional p → q is false only when p is true and q is false.
notes.simple: Think of p and q as statements. The symbols tell you whether to say “not,” “and,” “or,” “if…then,” or “if and only if.”
examples: If p means “it is raining,” then ~p means “it is not raining.”
If p means “it is raining” and q means “the road is wet,” then p → q reads “If it is raining, then the road is wet.”
steps: Name the statements using letters such as p and q.
Read the operator symbol between or before the letters.
For a conditional, identify the antecedent (the part after “if”) and the consequent (the part after “then”).
For converse, inverse and contrapositive, use the original conditional p → q: converse q → p; inverse ~p → ~q; contrapositive ~q → ~p.

notes.checkAnswer: A conditional p → q is false only when p is true and q is false.

notes.title: Understanding conditionals and their related statements
notes.answer: For p → q, the converse is q → p, the inverse is ~p → ~q, and the contrapositive is ~q → ~p.
notes.explanation: A conditional p → q is false only when p is true and q is false. The converse, inverse and contrapositive are made by swapping or negating the parts in specific ways.
notes.simple: A conditional is an “if p, then q” statement. Its converse swaps p and q; its inverse negates both; its contrapositive swaps and negates both.
examples: For p → q, the converse is q → p.
For p → q, the contrapositive is ~q → ~p.
steps: For p → q, identify p as the antecedent and q as the consequent.
Converse: swap the two parts, giving q → p.
Inverse: negate both parts, giving ~p → ~q.
Contrapositive: swap the parts and negate both, giving ~q → ~p.

notes.title: How to build a mathematical proof
notes.answer: A mathematical proof is a logical sequence of steps that establishes that a statement is correct.
notes.explanation: A mathematical proof is a chain of clear, valid steps that shows why a statement must be true. For example, if x is odd, write x = 2k + 1 for an integer k, then use algebra to show that x² has the form 2m + 1. For a set identity, start with an arbitrary element and show that it belongs to both sides.
notes.simple: A proof is a series of steps that gives a reason a mathematical statement is true.
examples: If x = 2k + 1, then x² = 2(2k² + 2k) + 1, so x² is odd.
To prove two sets are equal, prove that each set is a subset of the other.
steps: Start with what the question tells you.
Use a definition, such as x = 2k + 1 for an odd integer.
Work through clear algebraic or logical steps.
Connect the result to the definition of what you need to prove.

notes.checkAnswer: Write x = 2k + 1 for some k ∈ Z. Then x² = 2(2k² + 2k) + 1, so x² is odd.

notes.title: Theorems, conjectures and axioms
notes.answer: A theorem is proved, while an axiom is accepted as true without proof.
notes.explanation: A theorem is proved using known facts. A conjecture is believed to be true but has not been proved. An axiom is accepted as true without proof. A postulate is also accepted without proof, but is associated explicitly with geometry.
notes.simple: A theorem has been proved. A conjecture is still waiting for a proof. An axiom is a starting fact accepted without a proof.
examples: The sum of the interior angles of a quadrilateral is 360 degrees: theorem.
Every even integer greater than 2 is a sum of two prime numbers: conjecture.
steps: Read the statement carefully.
Ask whether it has been proved from previously known facts.
If it has, call it a theorem.
If it is believed true from observations but has not been proved, call it a conjecture.
If it is accepted as true without proof as a starting fact, call it an axiom.
notes.checkQuestion: What is one difference between a theorem and an axiom?
notes.checkAnswer: A theorem is proved; an axiom is accepted as true without proof.

notes.simple: Start with the left-hand side. Change it one correct step at a time until it becomes the right-hand side.
